slots.practicalActivity: Install kubectl and confirm it talks to a real cluster (even a cloud-provided sandbox or an existing one) with `kubectl cluster-info` and `kubectl get nodes -o wide`; for each node and each line of `cluster-info` output, write down whether it's a control-plane component (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) or something that runs on every node (kubelet, kube-proxy).
slots.deliverable: A terminal transcript of `kubectl cluster-info` and `kubectl get nodes -o wide` with a short written mapping of each component seen to control-plane vs. node.

slots.practicalActivity: Install kind or minikube and create a real local cluster from scratch (`kind create cluster` or `minikube start`), confirm `kubectl get nodes` shows a Ready node, then delete it and recreate it once more to prove the process is repeatable, not a one-time fluke.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of `kubectl get nodes` showing a Ready node from a local cluster the student created themselves, torn down and recreated at least once.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply a simple nginx Pod with `kubectl apply -f`, inspect it with `kubectl get pods -o wide` and `kubectl describe pod`, then deliberately break it (apply a version with a nonexistent image tag) and use the Events section of `describe` plus `kubectl logs` to diagnose exactly what went wrong before fixing it.
slots.deliverable: A terminal transcript showing `apply`, `get -o wide`, a `describe` Events section pinpointing a deliberately introduced failure, and `logs`/`exec` output after the fix.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a Pod manifest entirely by hand (apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec) for an nginx container, apply it, then change one field (e.g. an image tag or a label) and re-apply, using `kubectl diff -f` right before the second apply to see exactly what Kubernetes will reconcile in place rather than delete-and-recreate.
slots.deliverable: A hand-written Pod YAML plus `kubectl diff` and `kubectl apply` output showing an in-place declarative update to an already-running object.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a two-container Pod manifest (an nginx main container plus a busybox sidecar) sharing an emptyDir volume, apply it, then `kubectl exec` into the sidecar and curl `localhost` on the main container's port to prove they genuinely share one network namespace, and write a file from one container's shell that the other can read from the shared volume.
slots.deliverable: A two-container Pod YAML plus terminal proof the sidecar can curl the main container over localhost and read a file the main container wrote to the shared volume.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a Deployment for a sample product-catalog app with 3 replicas, apply it, kill one Pod directly with `kubectl delete pod` and watch the ReplicaSet recreate it within seconds, then use `kubectl scale` to go to 5 replicas and back down to 3.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing 3/3 Pods ready, a Pod killed and automatically replaced, and a successful `kubectl scale` up to 5 and back down to 3.

slots.practicalActivity: Change the Deployment's image tag and `kubectl apply`, watching `kubectl rollout status` track the rolling update; then deliberately set a bad/nonexistent image tag, watch the rollout stall, and run `kubectl rollout undo` to confirm it restores the last working revision.
slots.deliverable: A terminal transcript of a successful rolling update, a deliberately broken rollout, and a confirmed `kubectl rollout undo` restoring the previous working version.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy a 3-replica StatefulSet (e.g. a small postgres or redis image) behind a headless Service, confirm the stable ordinal Pod names (-0, -1, -2) and one PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod with `kubectl get pods,pvc`, then delete one Pod and confirm its replacement keeps the same name and reattaches the same volume.
slots.deliverable: `kubectl get pods,pvc` output showing ordinal-named Pods each with their own PVC, plus proof a deleted Pod's replacement reused the identical name and PVC.

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy a DaemonSet and confirm one Pod lands on every node with `kubectl get pods -o wide`; create a one-off Job that runs a batch task to completion; then create a CronJob on a short real schedule (e.g. every minute) and watch `kubectl get jobs` collect at least two triggered runs.
slots.deliverable: `kubectl get daemonset -o wide` showing one Pod per node, a completed Job's status, and a CronJob's `kubectl get jobs` history showing 2+ scheduled runs.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Workloads: deploy a realistic multi-workload stack in one apply for Northbridge Retail's product-catalog — a Deployment for the stateless app, a StatefulSet for a backing cache, and a CronJob for a nightly cleanup task — then kill a Pod from each and confirm each controller's self-healing behavior differs correctly (brand-new Pod vs. recreated-with-identity).
slots.deliverable: One combined apply of a Deployment, a StatefulSet, and a CronJob, with terminal proof each self-heals correctly after `kubectl delete pod`.

slots.practicalActivity: Expose the product-catalog Deployment with a ClusterIP Service, then from a temporary debug Pod curl it by both its cluster DNS name (`product-catalog.default.svc.cluster.local`) and its ClusterIP; create a second Service as NodePort and curl it from outside the cluster using a real node IP.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of a successful curl via the Service's DNS name from inside the cluster, and a successful curl to the NodePort from outside it.

slots.practicalActivity: Install a real Ingress controller (ingress-nginx, via its published install manifest) on the cluster, write an Ingress resource routing `/catalog` and `/checkout` to two different Services, and curl both paths through the Ingress's one external address.
slots.deliverable: A working Ingress resource plus curl output proving both `/catalog` and `/checkout` correctly route to their own Services through one Ingress.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply a default-deny NetworkPolicy in a namespace and confirm a Pod that could previously reach another now can't; then add a specific allow NetworkPolicy permitting only product-catalog to reach checkout on its port, and confirm an unrelated Pod stays blocked while product-catalog succeeds.
slots.deliverable: Three captured curl attempts (before default-deny, after default-deny, after the specific allow rule) with their differing, correct results.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Networking & Services: build the full networking path for checkout — a ClusterIP Service, an Ingress exposing it at `/checkout`, and a NetworkPolicy restricting which other Pods may reach it directly — then verify from both inside and outside the cluster that only intended traffic gets through.
slots.deliverable: One combined Service + Ingress + NetworkPolicy configuration with terminal proof of allowed external Ingress traffic and blocked unauthorized pod-to-pod traffic.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a ConfigMap holding non-sensitive settings (LOG_LEVEL, CATALOG_SERVICE_URL) and a Secret holding a fake DB password, mount both into a Pod via `envFrom` and `secretKeyRef`, confirm with `kubectl exec ... env` that both values appear correctly, and inspect `kubectl get secret -o yaml` to see the base64-encoded value and explain in writing why that is not encryption.
slots.deliverable: A running Pod whose `env` output (via `kubectl exec`) shows values from both a real ConfigMap and a real Secret, plus the base64 Secret YAML and a one-sentence note on why base64 isn't encryption.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a PersistentVolumeClaim, mount the resulting volume into a Pod, write a file to the mounted path, delete the Pod entirely, recreate it against the same PVC, and confirm the file is still there.
slots.deliverable: Terminal proof that a file written to a PVC-backed volume survives Pod deletion and recreation.

slots.practicalActivity: Inspect the cluster's default StorageClass with `kubectl get storageclass`, write a PVC that requests storage with no pre-created PersistentVolume (relying on dynamic provisioning), apply it, and confirm with `kubectl get pv,pvc` that a PersistentVolume was automatically created and bound.
slots.deliverable: A dynamically-provisioned PVC manifest plus `kubectl get pv,pvc` output showing an automatically created, Bound PersistentVolume.

slots.practicalActivity: Add CPU/memory requests and limits to the checkout Deployment and confirm them with `kubectl describe pod`; add a liveness and a readiness probe hitting a real HTTP path, then deliberately break the readiness probe's path and confirm with `kubectl get endpoints` that the Pod drops out of the Service while staying Running (not restarted).
slots.deliverable: `kubectl describe pod` output showing configured requests/limits, plus proof a failing readiness probe removes a Pod from Service Endpoints without killing it.

slots.practicalActivity: Confirm metrics-server is running, create an HPA targeting the checkout Deployment at 70% CPU utilization with minReplicas 3 / maxReplicas 10, generate real CPU load against it, and watch `kubectl get hpa -w` scale replicas up under load and back down once load stops.
slots.deliverable: A captured `kubectl get hpa` transcript showing replica count actually rising under generated load and falling back down after load stops.

slots.practicalActivity: On a real managed cluster, deploy enough replicas that Pods go Pending from insufficient node capacity and confirm a configured cluster autoscaler adds nodes; if no managed cluster is available yet, write the exact `az aks nodepool update --enable-cluster-autoscaler` or EKS Cluster Autoscaler configuration that would trigger this, with a written explanation of the scale-up trigger.
slots.deliverable: Either real `kubectl get nodes` output showing node count increase after Pending Pods, or a complete, correct cluster-autoscaler configuration with a written explanation of what triggers it.

slots.practicalActivity: Taint a node with `kubectl taint nodes <node> dedicated=batch:NoSchedule`, confirm a normal Deployment's Pods avoid it, add a matching toleration to a Job's Pod spec and confirm it schedules there anyway, then add podAntiAffinity to the checkout Deployment and confirm with `kubectl get pods -o wide` that replicas spread across different nodes.
slots.deliverable: Terminal proof of a tainted node avoided by untolerated Pods and accepted by a Pod with a matching toleration, plus `kubectl get pods -o wide` showing anti-affinity actually spreading replicas across nodes.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Scaling & Reliability: load-test the checkout Deployment end to end — requests/limits set, an HPA watching CPU, and anti-affinity spreading replicas across nodes — and narrate what `kubectl get hpa,pods -o wide -w` shows happening as real generated load ramps up and back down.
slots.deliverable: A combined Deployment (requests/limits + affinity) and HPA, with a captured transcript of replica count and node spread changing live under generated load.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real `checkout` namespace and move the checkout Deployment into it, then create a second, identically-named Deployment in a different namespace and confirm with `kubectl get deployments -A` that both exist independently without colliding.
slots.deliverable: Two same-named Deployments running in two different real namespaces, confirmed independent with `kubectl get deployments -A`.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a Role scoped to the checkout namespace granting only get/list/watch on pods and pods/log, bind it with a RoleBinding to a real user or ServiceAccount, and verify least-privilege with `kubectl auth can-i` for both an allowed action and a denied one (e.g. delete secrets).
slots.deliverable: A Role + RoleBinding manifest plus two `kubectl auth can-i` outputs — one correctly returning yes, one correctly returning no.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a dedicated ServiceAccount for checkout's Pods (instead of relying on `default`), attach it via `serviceAccountName` and confirm with `kubectl describe pod` that it's actually mounted; then label the checkout namespace with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`, apply a Pod spec that violates it (runs as root, privileged) and confirm it's rejected, and fix the spec (runAsNonRoot, dropped capabilities) to get it admitted.
slots.deliverable: `kubectl describe pod` output proving a custom ServiceAccount (not `default`) is attached, plus terminal proof of a Pod Security Standards rejection followed by a corrected spec being admitted.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Security & Access: lock down the checkout namespace completely — its own namespace, a dedicated ServiceAccount, a least-privilege Role+RoleBinding, and the restricted Pod Security Standard — then prove with `kubectl auth can-i` and a rejected Pod spec that the lockdown actually works, not just that the YAML applied.
slots.deliverable: One combined namespace+ServiceAccount+RBAC+Pod-Security configuration with terminal proof of both an allowed and a denied action.

slots.practicalActivity: Using a free-tier or trial Azure subscription, run `az aks create` to provision a real AKS cluster, run `az aks get-credentials`, confirm `kubectl get nodes` against the real managed cluster, and add a second user node pool with `az aks nodepool add`.
slots.deliverable: `kubectl get nodes` output against a real AKS cluster the student provisioned, plus `az aks nodepool list` showing both the system and the added user node pool.

slots.practicalActivity: Using a free-tier or trial AWS account, provision a real EKS cluster with `eksctl create cluster` (or an eksctl config file), update kubeconfig with `aws eks update-kubeconfig`, and confirm `kubectl get nodes` against the real managed cluster.
slots.deliverable: `kubectl get nodes` output against a real EKS cluster the student provisioned, plus the eksctl config file used to create it.

lessons.title: Connecting Clusters to Cloud Identity & Registries

slots.practicalActivity: Push a real image to Azure Container Registry or Amazon ECR, configure the AKS/EKS cluster to pull from it using managed identity/IAM integration instead of a static imagePullSecret, deploy a Pod from that image and confirm it pulls successfully; then run `az aks get-upgrades` or the equivalent EKS upgrade-availability check against the live cluster.
slots.deliverable: A Pod successfully running an image pulled from a real cloud registry via managed identity/IAM (no static pull secret), plus real output from an upgrade-availability check against the live cluster.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Helm, add a real public chart repo (e.g. bitnami), `helm install` a real chart with `--values`, run `helm upgrade --set` to change one value, and `helm rollback` back to the prior revision, checking `helm history` at every step.
slots.deliverable: `helm history` output showing at least 3 revisions (install, upgrade, rollback) for one real release.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real Helm chart from scratch for product-catalog — Chart.yaml, values.yaml, and templates/ for Deployment+Service using `{{ .Values.* }}` placeholders — run `helm lint` and `helm template` to verify rendering, then `helm install` it with a custom values-dev.yaml.
slots.deliverable: A working, lint-passing Helm chart (Chart.yaml + values.yaml + templates/) installed into the cluster, with `helm template` output proving correct values substitution.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately break a Pod three different ways (bad image tag, a missing ConfigMap reference, a failing readiness probe) and diagnose each using only `kubectl describe pod` and `kubectl logs`, recording which Events line gave each cause away; then connect Argo CD to a Git repo holding one of this course's manifests and confirm it syncs automatically on a commit.
slots.deliverable: A written diagnosis log identifying the Events-section evidence for 3 distinct real Pod failures, plus a real Argo CD Application syncing a manifest from Git (or its correct manifest with sync policy explained).

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Run an Application on Kubernetes

slots.practicalActivity: Write the capstone's scope document for Northbridge Retail's product-catalog and checkout services: list every object type from this course the deployment will need (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA, NetworkPolicy, RBAC) and the specific acceptance criteria that define 'done.'
slots.deliverable: A written capstone scope/requirements document listing every Kubernetes object type to be used and explicit, checkable acceptance criteria.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the full capstone exactly as scoped: Helm charts for both product-catalog and checkout with Deployment/Service/Ingress/ConfigMap/Secret/HPA templates, environment-specific values files, installed into a real cluster with `helm install`, verified with `kubectl get pods,ingress,hpa`, and exercised with a real `helm upgrade` followed by a `helm rollback`.
slots.deliverable: Two installed Helm releases (product-catalog, checkout) confirmed healthy via `kubectl get pods,ingress,hpa`, plus a demonstrated `helm upgrade` and `helm rollback` cycle.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone build time continued: finish wiring RBAC, NetworkPolicies, and the restricted Pod Security Standard onto the capstone's namespace, and write the Argo CD Application manifest plus a RUNBOOK.md documenting CrashLoopBackOff triage and rollback steps for the deployed services.
slots.deliverable: The capstone namespace fully locked down (RBAC + NetworkPolicy + Pod Security Standard, each verified) plus a written RUNBOOK.md and Argo CD Application manifest.

slots.practicalActivity: Record a short screen-captured walkthrough (or write a structured portfolio writeup) demonstrating the finished capstone cluster live — `kubectl get all -n northbridge-retail`, a live HPA scaling demo, and a live `helm rollback` — framed as a portfolio piece to show in a job interview.
slots.deliverable: A portfolio artifact (recorded demo or written walkthrough with real terminal output) showing the capstone's Kubernetes deployment running live, ready to present in an interview.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can deploy, expose, scale, secure, and operate a real multi-service application on Kubernetes end to end — writing Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, RBAC, and HPAs by hand, packaging them as Helm charts, running on managed AKS and EKS clusters, and troubleshooting real Pod failures using only kubectl.
